questions.q: What were the major challenges of nation building faced by India after Independence?
answer: When India became independent in 1947, it faced three great challenges of nation building.

answer.text: The first was to shape a single nation out of a land of immense diversity of religions, languages, castes and regions, and to accommodate this diversity without letting it break the country apart. The trauma of Partition made this even harder.
The second was to establish and nurture democracy, by adopting a Constitution based on rights, universal suffrage and free elections, in a society that was largely poor and illiterate.
The third was to ensure the development and well-being of all, removing poverty and inequality so that the benefits of progress reached every section of society.
Alongside these, the immediate task of integrating over five hundred princely states, achieved chiefly by Sardar Patel, was accomplished.

answer: Meeting these challenges laid the foundations of the modern Indian nation.

questions.q: How was the integration of the princely states achieved after Independence?

answer.text: over five hundred princely states had to be integrated into India, a huge and delicate task led by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel.

list: Most rulers were persuaded to join India by signing an 'Instrument of Accession'
Patel used patient negotiation, appealing to their patriotism and offering privileges
Junagadh's accession to Pakistan was reversed through a referendum, and Hyderabad was integrated by police action
Kashmir acceded to India when it was attacked, and thus a united India was forged

questions.q: Why was the reorganisation of states on a linguistic basis undertaken, and what were its effects?

answer.text: there were strong demands to redraw state boundaries on the basis of language, and this was eventually accepted.

list: People wanted states where they could be governed and educated in their own language
The demand grew strong, notably after the formation of Andhra for Telugu speakers

answer.text: led to linguistic states in 1956, with important effects.

list: It made administration and education easier in a familiar language and strengthened democracy
Far from breaking up India, it accommodated diversity and made the union stronger by satisfying regional feeling
